title: `Float32` and `Float64` arithmetic: IEEE 754 between columns
verdict: IEEE 754 rounding for `+ - *`, and for `/` between two columns
description: Polars's user guide says `Float32` and `Float64` generally follow IEEE 754, with exceptions for NaN equality and order and for the sign of zero and NaN. The kernels for `+ - *` are the IEEE operations in both float types, so they round as IEEE 754 binary32 and binary64 do, to nearest with ties to even. `/` between two columns of equal length is the IEEE quotient too.
A length-1 divisor against a longer column (a literal on a frame of two rows or more) is divided by multiplying with its reciprocal, two roundings: polars-double-scalar-divisor and PL-3.

The guide promises no error bound for other computations unless a function says so, so it does not settle the rounding of the elementary functions or logarithms (polars-elem-rounding, polars-log-base).
reference: `rounding: TIE_TO_EVEN` for `+ - × /` on doubles (native `Float`). `fp32` arithmetic is refused in every profile until #417's stage 3.

evidence.note: The same section at tag py-2.1.0.

provenance.notes: Polars's user guide says it generally follows IEEE 754 for `Float32` and `Float64`, with two exceptions: any NaN equals any other NaN and is greater than every non-NaN value, and operations guarantee nothing about the sign of zero or NaN or a NaN's payload (a sort or group by may make every zero +0 and every NaN a positive NaN). It promises no error bound unless a function says otherwise. The user guide is not versioned; the section reads the same at tag py-2.1.0.

evidence.note: Literal kernels: `x + c`, `x * c`, with shortcuts that return `x` for `c = 0` (add, subtract) and `c = 1`, exact.
`prim_true_div` is `l / r`; `prim_true_div_scalar` multiplies by `1 / rhs`. One macro for pf16, f32, f64.

notes: Raises `fp.arith` rounding to source: `+ - *` are the IEEE operations for `f32` and `f64`, column by column and with a literal (whose shortcuts return `x` exactly). The streaming engine runs the same polars-expr kernels.

Corrects the `/` claim: IEEE only when both sides are columns of equal length (or both have length 1). With a length-1 divisor against a longer side, `x / c` is `x * (1 / c)`, which can miss by an ulp (`49.0 / 49.0` is 0.9999999999999999). Title, verdict and description now say so and link polars-double-scalar-divisor (PL-3).
